period: Roman, Hadrian (AD 117-138); last hieroglyphic inscription AD 394
summary: The doorway where the Nile is born from a cave, and where in AD 394 a priest carved the last hieroglyphs anyone has found.
look: West of the main temple, near the second pylon, a gateway stands in a wall: the Gate of Hadrian. On its inner wall a relief shows the Nile god Hapi crouching in a cave beneath piled rocks, ringed by a snake, pouring water from two jars; nearby a crocodile carries the body of Osiris. The last hieroglyphic inscription is a small graffito beside a figure of the Nubian god Mandulis on this gate; it is easy to miss, so ask a guard or guide. The large rocky island nearby is Bigeh.
story:
Hadrian's gateway opened towards Bigeh, the sacred island the Greeks called the Abaton, 'the place not to be entered', where Osiris was believed to lie buried. Only priests crossed over, and the island was to be kept quiet: no music, no shouting, no fishing or hunting near the god's tomb. Ancient writers repeated that no bird flew over it and no fish came near its shores.

The relief of Hapi is theology's map of the Nile. Egyptians knew the river came from far to the south, yet they placed its mythical source right here, in a cavern under the cataract, from which the flood was poured out each year.

On 24 August 394, the birthday of Osiris, a priest called Esmet-Akhom, son of a second priest of Isis, carved a figure of Mandulis on this gate with a short hieroglyphic text and a longer note in demotic: he made the figure for all time, he says, because the god had been kind to him. It is the last dated hieroglyphic inscription known. The last demotic inscription followed on Philae in 452.

After that, the temples closed and the scribes died out. For some 1,400 years nobody could read a single sign, despite many attempts, until Jean-Francois Champollion cracked the system in 1822 with the help of the Rosetta Stone and of an obelisk from this very island.
details: On the gate's inner wall: Hapi in his cave under the rocks, ringed by a snake, pouring the Nile from two jars.
Nearby, a crocodile swimming with the body of Osiris on its back.
The small, rather crude figure of Mandulis in a tall plumed crown, with the AD 394 graffito: ask a guard to point it out.
Look across the water to Bigeh island, the Abaton, Osiris's tomb.
fun_fact: The last person known to have written hieroglyphs signed off with a dedication to a Nubian god, not an Egyptian one.
narration:
You are at the Gate of Hadrian, a Roman doorway on the west side of the temple. It faced the next island, Bigeh, which the Greeks called the Abaton, the place no one may enter. Egyptians believed Osiris lay buried there. Only priests crossed over, and the island was meant to stay silent: no music, no shouting, no fishing.

Look at the relief on the inner wall. Under a pile of rocks, inside a cave ringed by a snake, the Nile god Hapi crouches and pours water from two jars. This is the source of the Nile as theology placed it: right here, under the cataract. Nearby, a crocodile carries the dead body of Osiris across the water.

Now the moment this gate is famous for. On the 24th of August, AD 394, the birthday of Osiris, a priest called Esmet Akhom carved a figure of the Nubian god Mandulis here, with a few lines in hieroglyphs. They are the last dated hieroglyphs anyone has found. A last note in demotic script followed on Philae in 452. Then the knowledge died. For about 1,400 years nobody could read a single sign, until Champollion cracked the code in 1822.

Look for the small, rather crude figure of Mandulis in his tall plumed crown. Those few scratches are the final words of a script that had lasted more than 3,000 years.

period: Roman, probably begun under Augustus; decorated under Trajan (AD 98-117)
summary: Fourteen columns by the water, a wooden roof long gone, and the postcard of Philae: Isis's grand river entrance, never finished.
look: On the east shore stands a rectangular pavilion about 15 by 20 metres and nearly 16 metres high: fourteen columns, four on each end and five on each side, joined by screen walls, with doorways in the east and west facades. It is open to the sky. Inside, on the screen walls, Trajan burns incense before Isis and Osiris.
story:
Archaeologists call it a hypaethral temple, from the Greek for 'under the sky'. It was the island's main entrance from the river, and probably sheltered the sacred barque of Isis when it landed on the east bank. The name comes from the reliefs inside showing the emperor Trajan as pharaoh, burning incense to Isis and Osiris, but most of the structure may be older, possibly from the reign of Augustus.

It was never finished. Each column carries a different, lavish composite capital, topped by a plain block over 2 metres high that was meant to be carved into a figure of the dwarf god Bes, as in the birth houses at Philae, Armant and Dendera. The carving never happened.

The roof was wood. Sockets in the stone architraves show where three timber trusses, each about 12.5 metres long, carried a gently vaulted roof: an unusual marriage of wood and stone in an Egyptian temple.

Locals call it Pharaoh's Bed. In the 1830s the Scottish painter David Roberts drew it under that name, and travellers have been sketching it ever since.
details: Above each capital, a tall plain block: it was meant to become a carved figure of Bes.
Compare the capitals: each is a different composite of plant forms.
Along the top of the architraves, look for the sockets that held the wooden roof trusses.
On the inner screen walls: Trajan as pharaoh burning incense before Isis and Osiris.
Stand at the water's edge and look back: this is the postcard view.
fun_fact: During the decades when the old dam flooded Philae, boats could glide right between the columns of this kiosk.
narration:
This is Trajan's Kiosk, the building on every postcard of Philae. Locals call it Pharaoh's Bed. It stands on the east shore, and that is the point: this was the island's grand entrance from the river, where the sacred boat of Isis came and went in procession.

Count the columns: fourteen, four along each end and five down each side, joined by low screen walls. It is nearly 16 metres high, and it has no roof. It did once. Look along the tops of the stone beams and you can find the sockets for big timber trusses that carried a gently curved wooden roof. Wood and stone together like that is rare in an Egyptian temple. Archaeologists use a Greek word for a temple like this, hypaethral, open to the sky.

It is named after the Roman emperor Trajan, because inside he appears as a pharaoh, burning incense before Isis and Osiris. But most of it may be older, from the time of Augustus. And it was never finished. Each capital is topped by a tall stone block that was meant to be carved into the dwarf god Bes. The sculptors never came back.

In the 1830s the Scottish painter David Roberts drew it as the Bed of Pharaoh. Now look up at those plain blocks above the capitals: that is where Bes was supposed to be.

summary: A small temple where the gods play music: Bes on harp and tambourine, a monkey on the lute, all for Hathor, goddess of joy.
look: East of the main temple, a few steps from Trajan's Kiosk, stands the small temple of Hathor: a front hall of columns and a ruined inner part. The reliefs worth finding are on the columns and screen walls of the front hall: musicians, dancers and offerings of drink.
story:
Hathor was the goddess of love, music, dancing and drunkenness, and on Philae she had a small temple of her own beside Isis. Its front hall is a party in stone. The dwarf god Bes, protector of homes and of childbirth, plays the harp and beats a tambourine; a monkey plays the lute; other figures play pipes and offer wine.

The theme comes from a myth. Hathor once stormed off to the south in fury as a lioness, and the gods had to coax her home to Egypt with music, dance and drink. Philae, on the southern border, was a natural place to welcome her back.
details: Bes, short, bearded and bandy-legged, playing a harp.
Bes again with a tambourine: Hathor's festivals were loud.
A monkey playing the lute among the musicians.
Figures offering jars of wine: drink was part of Hathor's worship.
fun_fact: One of Hathor's feasts was known as a Festival of Drunkenness: getting merry in her honour was a religious duty.
narration:
This small temple belongs to Hathor, goddess of love, music, dancing and, yes, drinking. Look at the reliefs in the front hall: it is a concert. The dwarf god Bes, bearded and bandy-legged, plays the harp and bangs a tambourine. A monkey plays the lute. Others blow pipes and offer wine.

There is a myth behind the music. Hathor once stormed off to the south as a furious lioness, and the gods had to coax her home with songs, dancing and drink. Philae, on the southern border, was the place to welcome her back. Find Bes with his harp first, then look for the monkey with the lute.

summary: Isis outlived the old gods elsewhere by well over a century here, thanks to Nubian peoples and a treaty, until Justinian ordered her temple closed.
look: The Christian layer is everywhere once you look for it: crosses cut into doorways and walls, gods with their faces hacked away, and a Christian altar in the hypostyle hall of the Isis temple, which became a church of St Stephen.
story:
In AD 298 the emperor Diocletian pulled Rome's frontier back to Philae and agreed to pay the Nobades and the Blemmyes, two peoples of the south, a yearly stipend in gold to keep the peace. Both worshipped Isis. So while temples were closing across the Christian empire, Philae stayed open. In 452 a treaty between the Roman commander Maximinus and the Blemmyes and Nobades still guaranteed them access to the cult image of Isis. The last hieroglyphic (394) and demotic (452) inscriptions were carved here.

Christians lived on the island too: by the mid-5th century there were several churches beside the temples. The historian Procopius says the end came under Justinian: his commander Narses destroyed the sanctuaries, put the priests under guard and sent the statues to Constantinople. The closure is dated to 537. Many scholars now argue, with Jitse Dijkstra, that organised worship had faded long before, since the last evidence of an active priesthood dates to the 450s.

Afterwards five temples were turned into churches, the temple of Isis becoming a church of St Stephen. The crosses and hacked faces you see are the scars.
details: In the hypostyle hall: crosses cut over the reliefs, and a Christian altar.
Gods with chiselled-out faces next to figures of Horus left untouched.
Small crosses scratched into door jambs by Christian worshippers.
Greek inscriptions from the church period among the reliefs; ask your guide to point one out.
fun_fact: Isis was still being worshipped here under a Roman treaty in 452, some 60 years after the emperor Theodosius had outlawed pagan sacrifice.
narration:
Look around and you will find crosses carved into these walls, and gods with their faces chiselled away. They tell how Philae became the last stand of the old religion.

In AD 298 the emperor Diocletian pulled Rome's border back to this island and paid two southern peoples, the Nobades and the Blemmyes, a yearly gift of gold to keep the peace. Both worshipped Isis. So while temples were closing all over the Christian empire, Philae stayed open for them. A treaty in 452 still guaranteed them access to the statue of Isis.

Christians lived here too, with several churches beside the temples. The historian Procopius says the end came under the emperor Justinian, around 537. His general Narses tore down the sanctuaries, put the priests under guard and sent the statues to Constantinople. Many scholars now think the old cult had already faded by then.

The temple of Isis became a church of Saint Stephen. Look for a cross cut right across an ancient relief, and notice which faces were hacked. Horus, oddly, is often spared.

summary: For decades visitors rowed through a half-drowned temple; then engineers drained the river, cut Philae into 40,000 pieces and rebuilt it on another island.
look: Stand at the edge of Agilkia and look out over the water: the original island of Philae lies about 500 metres away under the reservoir between the old dam and the High Dam. Agilkia was cut down and reshaped to copy Philae's outline, so the temples sit in the same relation to each other and to the water as before, but 12.4 metres higher. Look closely at any wall for the fine joints between reassembled blocks.
story:
When the British finished the first Aswan dam in 1902, its reservoir covered Philae for much of the year. The dam was raised again in 1907-1912 and 1929-1934, and the island emerged only when the sluices were open, from July to October. Visitors rowed between the capitals; plants and paint washed away and silt crusted the stone. Proposals to move the temples were rejected in favour of strengthening the foundations.

The High Dam (1960-1970) made it worse: Philae would sit permanently in water that rose and fell between the two dams. By the 1960s up to a third of the buildings were under water all year. UNESCO's Nubian campaign at first left Philae out, but international pressure brought it in, and a plan by Egyptian designers won the competition.

A coffer dam of two rows of steel plates, with a million cubic metres of sand between them, was built around the island and the water pumped out. Every structure was recorded by photogrammetry and cut into about 40,000 numbered blocks weighing 2 to 25 tons. The Egyptian High Dam Company levelled Agilkia and laid the foundations; the Italian firms Condotte and Mazzi Estero dismantled and rebuilt the 95 structures. The operation ran from 1977 to 1980.
details: Fine joints between the blocks: each of about 40,000 pieces went back to its numbered place.
From the island's edge, look towards the old island's site, about 500 metres away under the water.
Notice how the temples still sit right at the water's edge: Agilkia was reshaped to copy Philae.
On some lower walls, look for paler, washed-out reliefs: decades of flooding stripped their paint.
fun_fact: The European Space Agency's comet lander Philae aimed for a landing site named Agilkia in 2014; it bounced and came to rest about a kilometre away.
narration:
Everything around you has been taken apart and put back together. For almost 70 years this temple spent much of each year under water.

When the British finished the first Aswan dam in 1902, its lake rose over Philae. The dam was raised twice more, and the island only came out when the sluices opened in summer. Tourists rowed between the tops of the columns.

Then came the High Dam. Philae would now sit forever in water rising and falling between the two dams, grinding the stone. So in the 1970s engineers built a double wall of steel plates around the island, filled it with sand, and pumped the inside dry. Every building was measured, photographed and cut into about 40,000 numbered blocks, some weighing 25 tons. Meanwhile nearby Agilkia island was cut down to match Philae's outline, about 12 metres higher. Italian firms rebuilt the temples, and the work was finished in 1980.

Look closely at a wall near you and find the fine joints between the blocks. Each one went back exactly where it came from.

period: Opened 1997; collections from prehistory to the 20th century
summary: Built to hold what was saved when Lake Nasser drowned Nubia: the story of Egypt's southern neighbour in one walk.
look: The building, in local sandstone and granite, steps down a steep slope like a Nubian village, set in a large landscaped garden. Inside, a big main hall holds the largest monuments, and the galleries run in order from prehistory through the Nubian kingdoms, Egyptian rule, the Kushite pharaohs, Meroe, Christian and Islamic Nubia, ending with Nubian village life. Outside, paths lead past a reconstructed Nubian house and other open-air displays. Allow about two hours.
story:
Egypt asked for this museum in 1960, when the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia began. The High Dam's lake was about to cover Lower Nubia, and archaeologists from all over the world raced to excavate and rescue what they could. The finds needed a home, and the Nubians a place for their memory. A trust fund from donor states and the governments of Egypt and Sudan paid for it.

The Egyptian architect Mahmoud El-Hakim designed it, and it opened on 23 November 1997. In 2001 it won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture. The site covers about 50,000 square metres, of which 7,000 are building, on three floors with a library and documentation centre. Around 3,000 objects were registered for it, from geology and prehistory through Pharaonic, Roman, Coptic and Islamic times to the history of Aswan.

Why does Nubia deserve a museum of its own? Because it was the corridor between Egypt and the rest of Africa, a source of gold, ivory, ebony and incense, and home to kingdoms that rivalled Egypt and once ruled it. This museum lets you see that story from the Nubian side. It is air-conditioned, which makes it a good midday visit.
details: From the entrance, look at the building itself: stepped sandstone volumes echoing a Nubian village.
In the main hall, the colossal statues: check each label for the site it was rescued from.
Follow the galleries in order; the labels give the period for each case.
In the garden, the reconstructed Nubian house and its painted entrance.
fun_fact: Only about 7,000 of the site's 50,000 square metres are building; the rest is garden, so leave time to wander outside.
narration:
Welcome to the Nubian Museum. It exists because of a flood. When Egypt built the High Dam in the 1960s, the lake behind it was going to drown Lower Nubia, the whole valley between Aswan and the Sudanese border, with its temples, cemeteries and villages. Archaeologists from all over the world rushed to dig and rescue what they could, and Egypt asked UNESCO for a museum to keep it. This is the result, opened in 1997.

Notice the building first. The architect, Mahmoud El Hakim, used local sandstone and granite and stepped it down the slope like a Nubian village. It won the Aga Khan Award for Architecture.

Why Nubia? It was the corridor between Egypt and the rest of Africa. Gold, ivory, ebony and incense all came north through it. The Egyptians called it Ta Seti, the Land of the Bow, after its famous archers. For 3,000 years Egypt and Nubia traded, fought, intermarried and took turns conquering each other.

The galleries run in order: prehistory, the early Nubian cultures, the kingdom of Kerma, Egyptian rule, the Kushite kings who became pharaohs, Meroe, Christian and Islamic Nubia, and finally Nubian village life. Give it about two hours, then walk the garden. Start in the main hall, and look up at the biggest statue there.

summary: Egypt's southern neighbour, rival, colony and conqueror: the Land of the Bow, whose kings once ruled Egypt and built more pyramids than the pharaohs.
look: No single object here: use this as the key to the museum. On any map of the Nile find the cataracts. Lower Nubia lay between the First and Second Cataracts, now largely under Lake Nasser; Middle and Upper Nubia, the heartland of Kush, lie upstream in Sudan, as far as the meeting of the Blue and White Niles at Khartoum.
story:
Nubia is the Nile valley between the First Cataract and Khartoum. The Egyptians called it Ta-Seti, 'the Land of the Bow', after its archers. Egyptian texts distinguished Wawat, the north, from Kush, the south.

The two peoples were intertwined from the start. Around 3100 BC rulers of the A-Group culture were buried at Qustul with real wealth, until Egypt's First Dynasty apparently destroyed them. From about 2500 BC the kingdom of Kerma grew into a power that controlled the valley from the First to the Fourth Cataract and raided deep into Egypt. Egypt built fortresses against it and, around 1500 BC under Thutmose I, conquered it; for nearly five centuries Egyptian viceroys ran Nubia for its gold and built temples like Abu Simbel.

Then the tables turned. In the 8th century BC the kings of Kush, ruling from Napata, conquered Egypt as the 25th Dynasty, until Assyria drove them out. The kingdom moved its centre south to Meroe and lasted until the 4th century AD. Three Christian kingdoms followed, Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia; Makuria fought off the Arab armies in 652 and kept a treaty with Egypt for some 600 years. From the late Middle Ages Nubia became Muslim.

Nubians live on, with their own languages. Each raising of the old dam drowned villages, and the High Dam displaced about 100,000 Nubians in Egypt and Sudan.
details: On the museum's maps, find Qustul, Kerma, Napata and Meroe: the four great centres in order.
Look for bows and arrowheads: the archers who gave Ta-Seti its name.
Compare faces: Nubians in Egyptian art are shown with darker skin, short curled hair and distinctive dress.
Watch for objects that mix the two styles: Egyptian gods in Nubian hands, Nubian pottery in Egyptian graves.
fun_fact: Sudan has more pyramids than Egypt: over 200 at Meroe alone, steeper and narrower than those at Giza.
narration:
Here is Nubia in a few minutes, so the museum makes sense. Nubia is the Nile valley south of Aswan, from the First Cataract to around Khartoum. The Egyptians called it Ta Seti, the Land of the Bow, because Nubian archers were the best they knew.

Think of Egypt and Nubia as two neighbours who never stopped arguing. Around 3100 BC Nubian chiefs at Qustul were buried with real wealth, until Egypt's first kings crushed them. Then the kingdom of Kerma rose in Sudan and grew strong enough to raid deep into Egypt. Egypt answered with fortresses and, around 1500 BC, with conquest: viceroys, gold mines, and temples like Abu Simbel.

Then the tables turned. In the 8th century BC the kings of Kush marched north and ruled all Egypt as pharaohs, the 25th Dynasty, until the Assyrians drove them home. They moved their capital south to Meroe and built more pyramids than Egypt ever did. Later came Christian Nubian kingdoms that fought off the Arab armies and then kept the peace by treaty for 600 years, and finally Islam.

Nubians are still here, with their own languages. In the 1960s about 100,000 of them in Egypt and Sudan lost their homes to the lake behind the High Dam. As you walk the galleries, watch how Egyptian and Nubian styles keep borrowing from each other.

period: A-Group, 4th millennium BC to about 2900 BC
summary: Pottery as thin as eggshell and a royal incense burner that started an argument: was Egypt's kingship born in Nubia?
look: The first galleries cover Nubia before writing: stone tools, images of cattle and wild animals, and A-Group pottery. Look for two kinds: eggshell ware, with walls only millimetres thick, often painted with patterns that resemble basketry, and black-topped red ware, polished red pots with a black rim.
story:
George Reisner named this culture the 'A-Group' in 1907, a label now outdated but still used. Its people lived between the First and Second Cataracts, from Kubaniyya near Aswan to Buhen: semi-nomadic herders, fishers and hunters who began farming late in the 4th millennium BC. They grew rich as middlemen, trading incense, ebony, ivory, carnelian and gold north for Egyptian goods, which ended up in their graves.

Their potters were superb. Eggshell ware has impossibly thin walls. Black-topped red ware was fired red, then the hot rim was dipped in sawdust to starve it of oxygen and turn it black.

In 1960-64, before the lake rose, the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute excavated the royal Cemetery L at Qustul, near Abu Simbel. One grave held nearly 200 vessels. Bruce Williams studied an incense burner from it carved with royal imagery and suggested kingship might have developed in Nubia first. Most scholars disagree: older royal images from Egypt itself suggest the Qustul rulers adopted Egyptian symbols. Around 2900 BC the A-Group disappears, apparently destroyed by Egypt's First Dynasty.
details: Eggshell ware: find the thinnest bowl in the case; its walls are only millimetres thick.
Black-topped red pots: the black rim came from dipping the hot pot in sawdust.
Images of cattle and wild animals: the world of Nubian herders and hunters.
Any object labelled Qustul: the A-Group royal cemetery near Abu Simbel, now under Lake Nasser.
fun_fact: At Nabta Playa in the desert west of Abu Simbel, prehistoric people set up a stone circle that may be one of the world's first astronomical devices, about 2,000 years before Stonehenge.
narration:
These first rooms show Nubia before history, and the star here is pottery. Look for two kinds. Eggshell ware has walls only millimetres thick, so fine it is hard to believe it was made without a wheel. Black-topped red ware was polished red, then its rim was dipped in sawdust while hot, starving it of oxygen and turning it black.

The people who made them have a dull name, the A-Group, given by the archaeologist George Reisner in 1907. They lived between the First and Second Cataracts, herding, fishing and hunting, and they grew rich as middlemen, passing incense, ebony, ivory and gold north to Egypt.

Their chiefs were buried at Qustul, near Abu Simbel. An incense burner from one royal grave carries royal symbols, and one scholar suggested that kingship might have begun here, not in Egypt. Most experts disagree, because older royal images exist in Egypt itself. Around 2900 BC the A-Group vanished, probably crushed by Egypt's first kings. Now find the thinnest bowl in the case.

period: C-Group about 2400-1550 BC; Kerma about 2500-1500 BC
summary: Cattle herders, desert archers and the first great kingdom of inner Africa, which once invaded Egypt while the Hyksos held the north.
look: This section mixes several peoples. Look for C-Group bowls with incised geometric patterns and images of cattle; weapons and grave goods of the desert archers; and Kerma pottery, thin polished beakers flaring like tulips, red with a black top.
story:
The C-Group (about 2400-1550 BC) were cattle herders in Lower Nubia. Cattle meant milk, blood, hides and status, and their stone-circle graves had offering chapels with stelae showing cattle and horns. Their neighbours included desert peoples known as the Pan-Grave culture, usually linked with the Medjay, archers whom Egypt hired as scouts and soldiers; in the New Kingdom 'Medjay' came to mean police.

Further south, at Kerma in Sudan, grew the first great kingdom of inner Africa. By its classic phase (1750-1500 BC) Kerma was a city of about 25 hectares with a huge mud-brick temple, the Western Deffufa, which still stands. Its kings were buried under great mounds with large numbers of human sacrifices. At its height Kerma controlled the Nile from the First to the Fourth Cataract.

Egypt was afraid of it. Middle Kingdom kings built forts at Buhen, Aniba, Kor and elsewhere, now under the lake. Kerma allied itself with the Hyksos, the foreign kings of northern Egypt, and an inscription in the tomb of Sobeknakht at El-Kab records a Kushite invasion deep into Egypt between about 1575 and 1550 BC; statues looted from Egypt were carried to Kerma. Around 1500 BC Thutmose I destroyed it.
details: C-Group bowls: incised geometric patterns, sometimes filled with white.
Images of cattle and horns: the C-Group's wealth walked on four legs.
Kerma beakers: tulip-shaped, red body, black rim, walls thin and polished.
Bows, arrowheads and daggers: the archers of the desert.
fun_fact: The Theban king Kamose caught a messenger in the desert carrying a letter from the Hyksos king to the ruler of Kush, inviting him to attack Egypt from the south and share the spoils.
narration:
This room is about the peoples who filled Nubia after the A-Group, and one of them nearly broke Egypt.

First, the C-Group, cattle herders from about 2400 BC. Cattle were their wealth: milk, blood, hides and status. They decorated graves and pottery with cattle, so look for horned animals scratched into stone and clay.

Next, desert archers known as the Medjay. Egypt hired them as scouts and soldiers, and later the word Medjay simply meant police.

Then the giant: the kingdom of Kerma, far south in Sudan. By 1750 BC Kerma was a real city, with a huge mud-brick temple that still stands. Its kings were buried under great mounds with many sacrificed servants. Egypt built fortresses to watch it. Around 1550 BC, while foreign Hyksos kings held the north of Egypt, Kerma invaded from the south. An Egyptian king even caught a messenger carrying a letter from the Hyksos king to the ruler of Kush, proposing an alliance. Around 1500 BC Egypt struck back and destroyed Kerma. Look for Kerma's tulip-shaped beakers, red with a black rim.

summary: When Egypt ruled Nubia: a viceroy called the King's Son of Kush, Nubian princes raised at court, and gold by the ring.
look: This section shows Nubia as an Egyptian province: statues and stelae of officials, temple pieces from sites now under Lake Nasser, and objects that blend Egyptian and Nubian styles. The colossal royal statues in the main hall belong to this chapter; check their labels for the sites they were rescued from.
story:
After Thutmose I destroyed Kerma around 1500 BC, Egypt governed Nubia for nearly five centuries. In charge was a viceroy who reported directly to pharaoh, first titled 'King's Son of the Southern Lands' and, from Thutmose IV's reign, 'King's Son of Kush'. Under him were two provinces: Wawat in the north, centred at Aniba, and Kush in the south, centred at Soleb and later Amara West. He had two deputies, scribes, an overseer of cattle and the priests of the Egyptian-built temples.

The prize was gold. The tomb of the viceroy Amenhotep, called Huy, at Thebes shows the tribute being counted and shipped north to the king. Among the Nubians in those scenes is Heqanefer, prince of Miam, who had been brought up at the Egyptian court and was buried in Nubia in an Egyptian-style tomb.

Pharaohs filled Nubia with temples, from Amada and Wadi es-Sebua to Abu Simbel; most were moved in the 1960s. Revolts flared for centuries, and after about 1070 BC, as Egypt weakened, the title King's Son of Kush faded away.
details: The colossal statues in the main hall: read the labels for where they once stood.
Statues or stelae naming a King's Son of Kush, Egypt's viceroy of Nubia.
Gold objects: rings, jewellery or ingots, the reason Egypt wanted Nubia.
Pieces where Egyptian and Nubian styles mix: Nubian faces and dress in Egyptian poses.
fun_fact: The name Nubia may come from nub, the Egyptian word for gold, though no ancient text actually uses it that way.
narration:
This part of the museum covers the centuries when Egypt ruled Nubia. Around 1500 BC Thutmose the First destroyed Kerma, and for nearly 500 years Egyptian control reached deep into Sudan.

The man in charge was a viceroy with a grand title: King's Son of Kush. He reported straight to the pharaoh and ran two provinces, Wawat in the north, roughly the area now under Lake Nasser, and Kush in the south.

What did Egypt want? Gold, above all. Nubia's deserts held the richest mines Egypt knew. In the tomb of one viceroy, Huy, at Thebes, the yearly tribute arrives and is counted for the king. Among the Nubians in those scenes is a prince called Heqanefer, raised at the Egyptian court, who was later buried at home in an Egyptian-style tomb.

Pharaohs also covered Nubia with temples, Abu Simbel among them, and most were moved in the 1960s to escape the lake. Look in this section for a statue or stela naming a King's Son of Kush, and ask yourself whether the face looks Egyptian or Nubian.

summary: Kings from Sudan who conquered Egypt, revived its ancient art and temples, and fought Assyria before being driven home.
look: Look for Kushite royal images: kings wearing a close-fitting cap crown with two cobras on the brow instead of one, with broad faces and strong necks. Look too for Amun as a ram, the god of Gebel Barkal, the holy mountain at Napata. Some pieces may be originals and some casts; trust the labels.
story:
After Egypt withdrew from Nubia, a new kingdom grew at Napata, beneath the sacred mountain of Gebel Barkal, where Thutmose III had founded a temple of Amun. Its kings worshipped Amun fervently. King Kashta took over Upper Egypt peacefully, and his daughter Amenirdis became God's Wife of Amun at Thebes.

His son Piye ruled from 744 BC. When Tefnakht of Sais led a coalition of Delta princes south, Piye marched north in his 20th year, arrived at Thebes in time for the Opet festival, took Hermopolis after a five-month siege and captured Memphis. His Victory Stela from Gebel Barkal tells how he made his soldiers purify themselves before battle, and how he was more upset that the horses of Hermopolis had been starved than by the rebellion itself. Then he went home and never returned.

His successors Shabaka, Shebitku, Taharqa and Tanutamun ruled from Memphis and Napata. Taharqa (690-664 BC) enjoyed a great flood and a building boom at Karnak, Kawa and Gebel Barkal, and was buried in the largest Nubian pyramid, at Nuri, with over 1,070 shabtis. These kings revived the styles of the Old and Middle Kingdoms on purpose. In 701 BC a Kushite army marched to help Hezekiah of Judah against Sennacherib; the Bible calls Taharqa Tirhakah. Assyria struck back: Esarhaddon took Memphis in 671 and captured Taharqa's family, and Ashurbanipal's army sacked Thebes in 663. Herodotus, writing in Greek more than two centuries later, remembered an 'Ethiopian' king Sabakos, Shabaka, who put criminals to work building embankments instead of executing them.
details: Two cobras on a king's brow: the sign of a Kushite pharaoh.
The close-fitting cap crown, typical of the Kushite kings.
Amun as a ram, or a ram's head: the god of Gebel Barkal.
Heavy, muscular royal statues that deliberately copy Old Kingdom models.
Taharqa's name in a cartouche; you will see his giant column at Karnak on the 22nd.
fun_fact: When the Assyrians took Memphis, they carried colossal statues of Taharqa home as trophies; pieces of three were found at the entrance of a palace at Nineveh.
narration:
This section is about the kings Greek writers called Ethiopians, often called today the Black Pharaohs: the rulers of Kush, from Napata in Sudan, who governed all of Egypt for most of a century.

They worshipped Amun as fervently as any Theban, and they saw Egypt as a land that had lost its way. In the 720s BC King Piye marched north, timed his visit to Thebes for Amun's great festival, besieged Hermopolis for five months and took Memphis. He ordered his soldiers to purify themselves before battle. And he loved horses: in his victory inscription he is angrier that the horses of Hermopolis were starved during the siege than about the rebellion itself. Then he sailed home and never came back.

His successors stayed. Shabaka, Shebitku, and above all Taharqa, who ruled from 690 to 664 BC and built at Karnak, where you will see his giant column on the 22nd. These kings deliberately revived the art of the pyramid age. Their armies fought Assyria in Palestine, and the Bible remembers Taharqa as Tirhakah.

In the end Assyria won. It took Memphis in 671 BC and sacked Thebes in 663, and the Kushites went home to build pyramids in Sudan. Look for a king with two cobras on his brow instead of one: that is the sign of a Kushite pharaoh.

period: Kingdom of Kush at Meroe, about 590 BC to AD 350
summary: Iron, ruling queens, an alphabet nobody fully understands, and a bronze head of Augustus buried under a temple step.
look: Look for fine painted Meroitic pottery, jewellery, offering tables and stelae carved in Meroitic script, an alphabet of 23 signs in two forms, one hieroglyphic and one cursive. Lion-headed figures represent Apedemak, Meroe's own war god.
story:
After the Assyrians, Kush turned south. King Aspelta possibly moved the capital from Napata to Meroe, between the Fifth and Sixth Cataracts, around 590 BC, and from about 280 BC the royal cemetery moved there too: more than 200 steep pyramids still stand. Meroe sat on iron ore and hardwood for fuel, and its iron industry led the scholar Archibald Sayce to call it 'the Birmingham of Africa', though modern scholars debate the scale.

Queens mattered. The king shared authority with the kandake, the queen mother, and some queens ruled. Meroe kept Egyptian gods such as Amun and Isis beside its own, like the lion-headed Apedemak.

In the 20s BC Meroitic forces raided Roman Egypt and carried off statues from the towns around Aswan. The prefect Petronius retaliated and sacked Napata, and a peace was agreed between Augustus and Queen Amanirenas. One looted bronze head of Augustus was buried under the steps of a temple at Meroe; it is now in the British Museum.

The Meroitic script has 23 letters derived from hieroglyphs. Scholars can read the sounds, but the language itself remains poorly understood.
details: Meroitic script on stelae or offering tables: hieroglyph-like signs or a flowing cursive, 23 letters in all.
Fine Meroitic pottery: thin, painted with plants and animals.
Lion-headed figures: Apedemak, the Meroitic god with no Egyptian twin.
Iron objects, the industry that made Meroe rich.
fun_fact: The Greek New Testament mentions a kandake: in Acts, Philip baptises the treasurer of 'Candace, queen of the Ethiopians', that is, of Meroe.
narration:
This room is Meroe, the last and longest chapter of ancient Kush. After the Assyrians pushed the Kushite pharaohs out of Egypt, the kingdom's centre shifted south to Meroe, far up the Nile in Sudan, and it lasted until the 4th century AD. Its kings and queens were buried there under more than 200 steep, narrow pyramids.

Iron helped make it rich. Queens had real power. The title kandake, queen mother, reached Greek as Candace, and the New Testament mentions the treasurer of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians.

One queen, Amanirenas, took on Rome. Meroitic raiders looted statues from the towns around Aswan, Rome hit back, and in the end she made peace with Augustus. A bronze head of Augustus, taken in the raids, was buried under the steps of a temple at Meroe, perhaps so that everyone who went in walked over the emperor. It is now in the British Museum.

Look for writing in Meroitic script, an alphabet of 23 letters borrowed from hieroglyphs. Scholars can sound it out, but most of the words are still not understood.
